concepts.desc: What actually serves a person over time, even when it is not what they want now. The Kaṭha names it as one of two things that 'approach' every human being.

teaches.why: Names the good and the pleasant as two different ends that bind a person differently.
The steady one examines both and chooses the good over the pleasant.
Yama praises Naciketas for refusing every pleasant offer.

contrasts.why: Kaṭha sets the two side by side: one leads to the good, the other falls short of the goal.

concepts.desc: What gratifies now: wealth, praise, comfort, agreement. Not evil in itself, but binding when it is chosen for its own sake.

teaches.why: The pleasant is the second of the two roads.
The dull choose the pleasant for the sake of getting and keeping.
Yama offers long life, sons and wealth to turn Naciketas from his question.
Naciketas: these pleasures last till tomorrow and wear out the vigour of the senses.

concepts.desc: Separating the good from the merely pleasant, the real from the apparent. The Kaṭha's verb is vivinakti: the steady one 'examines and separates'. Śaṅkara compares it to the swan that separates milk from water.

teaches.why: 'Examining both, the steady one separates them' (samparītya vivinakti).
With discernment the mind is held steady and the senses obey, like good horses.
Having examined the worlds won by works, the seeker turns away from them.

concepts.desc: Truthfulness in speech, and the Real itself. 'Truth alone triumphs, not untruth.'

teaches.why: Truth alone triumphs, not untruth; by truth the path to the divine is laid.
The face of truth is hidden by a golden vessel; the seeker asks for it to be uncovered.
The teacher's parting instruction begins: speak the truth.
Gautama accepts Satyakāma because he did not swerve from the truth about himself.

contrasts.why: Satyam eva jayate, nānṛtam: truth wins, untruth does not.

concepts.desc: Falsehood, including the convenient falsehood. The Praśna warns that one who speaks untruth withers to the root.

teaches.why: Sukeśa would rather say 'I do not know' than speak untruth, which withers a person to the root.
Untruth does not triumph.

concepts.desc: Knowledge in the sense that changes the knower, set against avidyā, the ignorance that mistakes the pleasant for the good.

teaches.why: Knowledge and ignorance lead far apart; Naciketas desires knowledge.
Crossing death by the one, one attains immortality by the other.

contrasts.why: 'Widely opposed and leading to different ends are these two: ignorance and what is known as knowledge.'

concepts.desc: Not mere lack of facts: the confident misreading of what matters. Its signature is thinking oneself wise.

teaches.why: Ignorance is the opposite road to knowledge.
Living in ignorance yet thinking themselves wise, they wander like the blind led by the blind.
The same verse, repeated in the Muṇḍaka.
Those who worship ignorance enter blinding darkness.

concepts.desc: The knowledge by which the imperishable is grasped, as distinct from all learning about it.

teaches.why: Two kinds of knowledge are to be known, the higher and the lower.
The higher is that by which the imperishable is attained.

contrasts.why: The Muṇḍaka opens its teaching with this division.

concepts.desc: All learning, including the Vedas themselves, when it is information about the goal rather than arrival at it.

teaches.why: The four Vedas and the six auxiliary sciences are counted as the lower knowledge.
Nārada has mastered every science, yet says: 'I know only the texts, not the Self.'
The Self is not attained by discourse, intellect or much learning.

concepts.en: knowing that one does not know
concepts.desc: The Kena's paradox of humility: it is understood by those who do not claim to understand it, and not understood by those who do.

teaches.why: 'If you think you know it well, you surely know very little.'
'I do not think I know it well, nor that I do not know it.'
'It is not understood by those who understand; it is understood by those who do not.'

concepts.desc: The pride of the one who thinks the victory, or the knowledge, is their own. In later texts this is ahaṃkāra.

teaches.why: The gods thought, 'This victory is ours, this glory is ours.'
Śvetaketu returns from study conceited, thinking himself learned, and stiff.
Thinking 'I know it well' is the mark of knowing little.

concepts.desc: The Kaṭha's chariot: the self is the rider, the body the chariot, the intellect the charioteer, the mind the reins, the senses the horses. The reins stay with the one who rides.

teaches.why: Know the self as the rider, the body as the chariot, the intellect as the charioteer, the mind as the reins.
One whose charioteer is discernment and who holds the reins of the mind reaches the end of the road.

concepts.desc: The horses of the chariot. Unreined, they run wherever their objects pull them.

teaches.why: The senses are the horses; their objects are the roads they run on.
Without discernment, the senses are like vicious horses.
The senses were made outward-turning, so one looks outward, not within.

concepts.desc: Attention turned back towards the one who attends. A rare steady person, 'eyes turned inward', sees the inner self.

teaches.why: A rare steady person, desiring immortality, turned the eye inward and saw the inner self.
The childish follow outward desires into the wide net of death.

concepts.desc: What one most essentially is: unborn, undying, the witness of every state.

teaches.why: The knowing Self is not born and does not die.
This Self is Brahman; it has four quarters.
One who sees all beings in the Self, and the Self in all, does not recoil from anyone.

concepts.desc: The ground of all that is, identical in the Upanishads' teaching with the Self.

teaches.why: 'All this is Brahman. This Self is Brahman.'
What speech cannot express but by which speech is expressed: know that to be Brahman.
'Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite.'

concepts.desc: The one who knows and can show. The Upanishads send the seeker to such a teacher, and warn that the truth taught by an inferior person is not understood.

teaches.why: Approach, fuel in hand, a teacher learned in the Veda and established in Brahman.
Taught by an inferior person, it is not well understood.

concepts.desc: Concentrated effort, here the effort of finding out for oneself. Varuṇa does not hand Bhṛgu the answer; he sends him to inquire.

teaches.why: Bhṛgu asks his father to teach him Brahman; he is given clues and told to seek, and he undertakes tapas.
Bhṛgu reaches a first answer, returns, and is told again: seek to know Brahman by tapas.

concepts.desc: Study and recitation as one's own practice, never to be neglected, paired in the Taittirīya with teaching others.

teaches.why: Every virtue is listed together with 'study and teaching'.
'Do not neglect your own study.'

concepts.desc: Prajāpati answers gods, humans and demons with the same syllable, Da, and each hears what they most need: self-restraint, giving, compassion.

teaches.why: To the gods, Da means 'restrain yourselves'.
To humans, Da means 'give'.
To the demons, Da means 'be compassionate'; the thunder repeats it.

concepts.desc: Desire as the seed of will and action: 'as one's desire is, so is one's will; as one's will, so one's deed.'

teaches.why: A person is made of desire; desire becomes will, will becomes deed, deed becomes destiny.
When all desires lodged in the heart fall away, the mortal becomes immortal.
The childish run after outward desires.

concepts.desc: Sanatkumāra's final teaching to Nārada: joy is in the boundless, not in the small.

teaches.why: 'The boundless is joy; there is no joy in the small.'
Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else: that is the boundless.

concepts.desc: Of two birds on one tree, one eats the sweet fruit and the other only looks on. The verse's word is abhicākaśīti, 'looks on'; the commentators call this witness the Self.

teaches.why: The other bird, not eating, looks on.
When the grieving bird sees the other, the Lord, its sorrow ends.

contrasts.why: Two birds, companions on one tree: one eats the sweet fruit, the other looks on.

concepts.en: the one who eats the fruit
concepts.desc: The bird that eats the sweet fruit: experience consumed for its taste, and the grief that follows.

teaches.why: One bird eats the sweet fruit.
Sunk on the same tree, the person grieves, deluded by helplessness.

concepts.desc: Beyond waking, dream and deep sleep: the Self in itself, 'peaceful, auspicious, non-dual'.

teaches.why: The Fourth is neither inward- nor outward-knowing; it is the Self, to be known.
The partless OM is the Fourth.
